_comment: Source-checked Florida classifications and a bounded South Florida pilot planting catalog. Verified dates record review of the linked evidence, not guarantees of plant identification or unchanged taxonomy. Additional source-linked facts and Atlas records were reconciled on 2026-10-17. Structured growing conditions use the linked horticultural sources; size and maintenance categories are practical screening estimates.
source: Florida Native Plant Society profiles with UF/IFAS and Kew clarifications
scope: Florida nativity; preliminary school-landscape suggestions within the 330–334 ZIP pilot. Site suitability is conditional, not inferred from ZIP alone.
planning_method: Sun and moisture are conservatively simplified from each linked profile. Wet means consistently wet soil; occasional inundation alone is not mapped to wet. Space is a planning estimate from mature spread: small generally up to 4 ft, medium up to 10 ft, large above 10 ft; vines need managed support. Maintenance is an app planning estimate from growth and care notes, not an official rating. All new plantings need establishment care and school/facilities approval.
wildlife_method: Documented means a cited feeding, host or shelter relationship. It is neither a high/medium/low ranking nor a count of animals that will visit a site. Unknown indicates this catalog has not checked a relationship, not that the plant has no ecological value.

species.wildlife_support_basis: Documented relationship in the linked source; not a measured campus outcome or comparative ranking.
species.why: Coontie is the Atala butterfly's only Florida-native larval host. Atala caterpillars can also use some nonnative cycads; planting coontie does not guarantee their arrival.
species.suitability_notes: Slow-growing cycad, typically 3–5 ft wide. Use nursery-grown plants in well-drained soil. Seeds, foliage and roots are toxic; choose a school-approved location. Water during establishment.
species.taxonomy_notes: Zamia floridana is an older name for Florida coontie. Zamia pumila is not automatically merged: Kew accepts a separate Greater Antillean species under that name, while some Florida references use it differently.

helps.text: Caterpillars of the atala butterfly eat its leaves, and butterflies and beetles visit its cones.

buying.avoid: Some plants sold as Zamia pumila come from the West Indies, not Florida. Ask for the Florida kind.
